item.stem: When struck, a crystal of an ionic compound fractures rather than bending. Which explanation best connects this behavior to the arrangement of particles in the solid?

choices.choice_text: The crystal consists of separate neutral molecules whose weak attractions allow them to pull apart when struck.
choices.rationale: Discrete-molecule misconception: an ionic crystal contains an extended array of ions, not separate neutral molecules. Its brittleness results from repulsion after lattice displacement, not weak attractions between molecules. Fix: Identify the particles as cations and anions before explaining how they interact.

choices.choice_text: Displacement of a layer can bring like-charged ions next to one another, and their repulsion causes the crystal to fracture.
choices.rationale: An ionic solid is an extended, repeating array of cations and anions. Displacing a layer can disrupt the favorable arrangement of opposite charges and place like charges close together, producing repulsion that splits the crystal.

choices.choice_text: Layers of ions slide freely while maintaining their attractive interactions, allowing the crystal to fracture.
choices.rationale: Sliding-versus-fracture confusion: freely sliding layers that maintain their attractions would explain deformation, not brittle fracture. In the ionic-lattice model, displacement can instead bring like charges together and create repulsion. Fix: Check whether your explanation predicts a change in shape or separation into pieces.

choices.choice_text: Displacement of a layer brings like-charged ions together, and their attraction pulls the crystal apart.
choices.rationale: Charge-interaction reversal: like-charged ions repel rather than attract. The displacement can cause fracture, but the force responsible is repulsion between newly adjacent like charges. Fix: Label the neighboring charges and determine whether their interaction is attractive or repulsive.

object.defect: Ionic solids are brittle because shifting a layer of the lattice brings ions of like charge next to each other, and their repulsion splits the crystal. Choice B states this. Choice A wrongly describes ionic solids as made of neutral molecules. Choice C describes layers sliding while still attracting, which is how malleable metals behave, not ionic crystals. Choice D says like charges attract, which is incorrect. The item is well posed, with exactly one correct answer.

item.stem: A student taps a small chisel against a crystal of potassium bromide, KBr. Instead of flattening or denting, the crystal shatters into smaller pieces with flat faces. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for this observation?

choices.choice_text: Solid KBr is made of individual neutral KBr molecules held together by weak forces, so the molecules separate easily when the crystal is struck.
choices.rationale: Discrete-molecule misconception: solid KBr has no separate KBr molecules, only one continuous array of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Shattering comes from repulsion after the lattice shifts, not from weak forces between molecules. Fix: Identify the particles as cations and anions before describing how they interact.

choices.choice_text: The blow shifts one plane of ions relative to the next so that K⁺ ions sit beside K⁺ ions and Br⁻ beside Br⁻, and the resulting repulsion splits the crystal.
choices.rationale: Solid KBr is an extended lattice of alternating K⁺ and Br⁻ ions. A small shift of one plane lines up like charges across the boundary, replacing attraction with repulsion, so the crystal separates along that plane instead of deforming.

choices.choice_text: Planes of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions glide past one another while each ion keeps oppositely charged neighbors, so the crystal breaks apart.
choices.rationale: Sliding-versus-fracture confusion: planes that glide while keeping attractive neighbors would let the solid change shape without breaking. In the ionic lattice, a shift instead aligns like charges and causes repulsion. Fix: Check whether your explanation predicts bending into a new shape or separation into pieces.

choices.choice_text: Shifting a plane of ions places like-charged ions side by side, and the attraction between those like charges pulls the crystal apart.
choices.rationale: Charge-interaction reversal: ions with the same charge repel rather than attract. The shift does bring like charges together, but repulsion between them is what drives the fracture. Fix: Label the charges on newly adjacent ions and decide whether they attract or repel.

item.stem: A potassium bromide (KBr) crystal is secured at its base, and a slowly increasing sideways force is applied to its upper surface. The sample develops a crack and separates into pieces. Which explanation connects this observation to the particle arrangement in KBr?

choices.choice_text: KBr consists of individual neutral molecules, and the applied force overcomes weak attractions between those molecules.
choices.rationale: Discrete-molecule misconception: solid KBr contains an extended ionic array rather than individual molecules. Fracture follows repulsion caused by displacement of that array, not the separation of weakly attracted molecules. Fix: Identify the charged particles and their extended arrangement before explaining the crack.

choices.choice_text: The ions move in freely sliding layers that preserve their attractions, and this sliding makes the sample split.
choices.rationale: Sliding-versus-fracture confusion: unrestricted sliding that preserves attractions predicts deformation rather than splitting. Displacement in an ionic crystal can instead create repulsive interactions between nearby ions of the same charge. Fix: Determine whether the proposed particle motion predicts deformation or fracture.

choices.choice_text: The sideways force moves similarly charged ions close together, and their mutual attraction tears the sample into pieces.
choices.rationale: Charge-interaction reversal: ions with the same charge repel; they do not attract one another. The proposed displacement can account for cracking, but the resulting interaction must be repulsive. Fix: Mark each neighboring ion’s charge and identify the force between them.

choices.choice_text: Shifting part of the repeating ionic array can place ions with the same charge near each other, causing repulsion that splits the sample.
choices.rationale: The repeating K⁺ and Br⁻ arrangement is held together by attractions between opposite charges. A shift can bring similarly charged ions close together, creating repulsive forces that cause separation rather than continued deformation.

item.stem: A pure ionic compound has a high melting temperature. Which particle-level model best explains this observation?

choices.choice_text: The solid consists of separate cation–anion pairs; melting requires breaking the strong attraction within every pair.
choices.rationale: The discrete-pair trap treats an ionic solid as separate molecules. Its ions instead participate in an extended lattice, and melting disrupts that collective arrangement rather than separating every pair into isolated ions. Fix: Check whether the model includes attractions extending beyond a single cation–anion pair.

choices.choice_text: Cations and anions form a repeating array; the high melting temperature results mainly from the large masses of the ions.
choices.rationale: The mass-for-attraction trap substitutes particle mass for interaction strength. A high melting temperature reflects the substantial energy needed to disrupt strong attractions in the lattice, not simply the masses of its ions. Fix: Identify the interactions that added thermal energy must overcome.

choices.choice_text: Cations and anions form an extended, repeating array; melting requires substantial energy to disrupt many strong attractions throughout the array.
choices.rationale: Oppositely charged ions attract throughout the three-dimensional lattice, not just within isolated pairs. Substantial energy is needed to disrupt this arrangement enough for the ions to move past one another, accounting for the high melting temperature.

choices.choice_text: The solid contains neutral atoms formed when cations and anions lose their charges; strong attractions between these atoms explain its high melting temperature.
choices.rationale: The neutrality trap confuses an electrically neutral solid with individually neutral particles. The total positive and negative charges balance, but the particles remain charged ions whose attractions stabilize the lattice. Fix: Distinguish the solid’s total charge from the charge on each constituent particle.

item.stem: Magnesium oxide, MgO, is used to line furnaces because it can remain solid while metals inside the furnace are molten. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for the lining’s resistance to melting?

choices.choice_text: MgO consists of individual Mg²⁺–O²⁻ pairs, and the strong attraction inside each independent pair makes the lining difficult to melt.
choices.rationale: The discrete-pair trap replaces the extended ionic lattice with isolated pairs. Melting disrupts the collective arrangement of ions rather than breaking apart independent MgO molecules. Fix: Check whether each ion interacts with multiple surrounding ions rather than only one partner.

choices.choice_text: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions occupy a repeating lattice, but their large particle masses are the main reason the lining resists melting.
choices.rationale: The mass-for-attraction trap attributes resistance to melting mainly to particle mass. The relevant energy requirement comes from disrupting strong electrostatic attractions throughout the lattice, not simply from having heavy particles. Fix: Identify which particle interactions must be disrupted when the solid melts.

choices.choice_text: The positive and negative charges cancel within MgO, leaving neutral atoms whose strong mutual attractions prevent the lining from melting.
choices.rationale: The neutrality trap mistakes overall electrical neutrality for neutral constituent particles. Balanced total charges do not remove the charges on Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; their electrostatic attractions hold the lattice together. Fix: Separate the sample’s net charge from the charge carried by each particle.

choices.choice_text: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions occupy a repeating three-dimensional lattice whose numerous strong electrostatic attractions require considerable energy to disrupt.
choices.rationale: Each ion interacts with surrounding ions in an extended structure. Overcoming enough of these strong attractions to allow the ions to move past one another requires substantial thermal energy, explaining why the lining withstands high temperatures.

item.stem: An ionic crystal fractures rather than bends when struck. A model represents the crystal as a repeating three-dimensional array of cations and anions. Which explanation best uses this model to account for the crystal’s brittleness?

choices.choice_text: A shift of ion layers brings oppositely charged ions together, and their repulsion causes the crystal to fracture.
choices.rationale: Charge-sign reversal: Oppositely charged ions attract rather than repel. Repulsion that contributes to fracture occurs when a shift brings like-charged ions close together. Fix: Identify the neighboring ions’ charge signs before deciding whether they attract or repel.

choices.choice_text: The crystal consists of separate neutral ion pairs, and a shift pulls these pairs apart by overcoming weak attractions between them.
choices.rationale: Discrete-pair misconception: An ionic crystal is an extended lattice, not a collection of separate neutral pairs. Each ion interacts with surrounding ions, so fracture must be explained using the lattice arrangement. Fix: Treat each ion as part of an extended array, not an isolated pair.

choices.choice_text: A shift of ion layers can bring like-charged ions next to one another, and their repulsion causes the crystal to fracture.
choices.rationale: The lattice arrangement ordinarily favors attractions between opposite charges while minimizing repulsions between like charges. Shifting a layer can disrupt this arrangement, bringing like charges close together so that repulsion separates parts of the crystal.

choices.choice_text: Ion layers slide while preserving their attractive interactions, allowing the crystal to bend without breaking.
choices.rationale: Unrestricted-sliding misconception: This predicts bending rather than the observed fracture. Shifting layers in an ionic lattice can bring like charges together instead of preserving favorable attractions. Fix: Check whether shifting a layer changes which charge signs become neighbors.

item.stem: A materials researcher passes a lithium fluoride crystal between rollers to make a thin sheet, but the crystal cracks instead of flattening. A particle model shows Li⁺ and F⁻ ions arranged in an extended, repeating three-dimensional lattice. Which explanation connects the arrangement of ions to the cracking observed during rolling?

choices.choice_text: Displacement of part of the lattice places Li⁺ beside F⁻, producing repulsion that separates portions of the crystal.
choices.rationale: Charge-sign reversal: Li⁺ and F⁻ attract because their charges have opposite signs. The repulsion responsible for cracking arises when displacement brings ions with matching charge signs close together. Fix: Compare the neighboring ions’ charge signs before identifying their interaction.

choices.choice_text: Rolling separates individual neutral LiF pairs by breaking the weak attractions holding those pairs together.
choices.rationale: Discrete-pair misconception: Solid lithium fluoride contains an extended ionic lattice, not independent neutral pairs held together weakly. Its response to rolling depends on interactions among ions throughout that lattice. Fix: Trace each ion’s interactions with surrounding ions rather than grouping ions into isolated pairs.

choices.choice_text: Rolling lets the ion layers move past one another without changing their attractive interactions, so the crystal forms an unbroken sheet.
choices.rationale: Unrestricted-sliding misconception: Unchanged attractions during sliding would support flattening, not the observed cracking. Displacing ionic layers can instead create unfavorable neighboring arrangements of like charges. Fix: Track which charge signs become neighbors after a layer moves.

choices.choice_text: Displacement of part of the lattice can place ions of the same charge beside each other, producing repulsion that separates portions of the crystal.
choices.rationale: The undisturbed lattice favors attractions between neighboring cations and anions and limits repulsions between like charges. Rolling can shift layers so that like-charged ions become neighbors, creating repulsion that contributes to cracking.
